hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) demonstrated the other night, of pointing out nothing but the evil. In my view our endeavour should be to give expression to criticism, not vindictively but in a friendly spirit, pointing out wherein there are errors, while at the same time giving credit where credit is due.
The hon. -member for Hants-Kings made the statement the other day that there was great prosperity in the country and that the chief point at issue was the question of distribution. He left us just there, making no attempt to show how the present method of distribution should be remedied. As I see it, that is.the whole question. The machines of Canada can produce more than the Canadian people can consume, although under present conditions they are not able to buy all the .products they require for their own necessities. The farming communities are confronted with this very problem. Consider the various processes through which the farmer's product passes, to each of which a profit is attached. The farmer takes his wheat to the elevator and there is a fixed charge there; the elevator stores it and there again there is a fixed charge; the railway company transports it and there is another fixed charge. And each one of these charges is based on a calculation which yields profits to those who handle the commodity. Not so with him. My hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) some years ago was engaged on behalf of a gas company to make a plea, which he did eloquently before the utilities commission, in relation to the price of gas for that company. He based his argument upon fixed charges, depreciation and also a fair profit, and in view of the argument, the utilities commission decided to have the price of gas fixed on the strength of these conditions. At that time the price of oats was twenty-five cents a bushel. I took home wth me the argument of my hon. friend from West Calgary and, calculating in accordance with the method which he had used in behalf of the gas company, I found that the price of oats should not be less than sixty cents a bushel. But in our agricultural communities it does not matter whether the grade of wheat is No. 1 or No. 2 or No. 4: the cost of handling the commodity is based on a system of profits and the farmer has to take just what is left. That is one of the reasons for the misdistribution of our so-called prosperity. Whenever there is a large crop the country at large prospers while the original producer does not get a fair share of what is left.
I come now to the Imperial conference, and in this regard I was interested in the argument of the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley). I gathered from the hon. gentleman this afternoon that in his opinion a sort of imperial parliament should mefet in London, the president of that parliament or committee to be the Prime Minister of Great Britain, with the representatives of the colonies sitting around, the assembly to solve foreign problems, questions of peace and war, and problems of foreign diplomacy. That very sane idea was put forward at the Imperial conference of 1911, when Sir Joseph Ward of New Zealand made such a proposal. Mr. Asquith, then Prime Minister of Great Britain, rose at once and observed that in matters of foreign policy and of peace and war the responsibility could never be shared. He held it was utterly opposed to the principle of responsible government and that the foreign policy of Great Britain must always be decided in Downing street, who were entirely answerable to the British people. These policies, the conduct of these affairs, he intimated, could never be the subject of shared responsibility. I have never seen any retraction of that statement. I know that Mr. Lloyd George confirmed the idea, and I know that in practice it is still carried out. When the treaty of Lausanne . was being negotiated we were not consulted, but were simply asked to sign on the dotted line after it had been negotiated. When the treaty of Locarno was negotiated we were not asked if we had anything to say about the matter, but after it was all completed we were asked to sign on the dotted line. Last year I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), whether Canada had been consulted in regard to sending warships to China. He said not a word. So that we are at war, whether we will it or no, when Great Britain is at war, but have nothing to say about the matter except that we are at war, as the hon. ex-leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Guthrie) said. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) says he does not like Canada to suffer from any inferiority complex, and he stated that the Prime Minister was suffering from an inferiority complex. He wanted matters to be settled by Canadians and did not want Canadian destinies to be settled in London. If that is so, then much more should we have something to say about questions of life and death and peace and war, especially when 60,000 of our Canadian boys lie in Flanders fields. The proposition that we should not have anything to say in re-

The Address-Mr. Adshead
gard to peace and war is one which no self-respecting Canadian can accept, and if the wedge is driven in, if the old country authorities are determined that we shall not have anything to say in this matter, it is they and not we who are driving the wedge between the motherland and the Dominion.
I was very thankful last year that the Prime Minister intervened at the last moment and granted us the last post fund under which Canada would not be so humiliated that we would have to go out in the streets and beg in order to provide funds enough to bury the indigent returned soldier. I thank the Prime Minister very much for dealing with that matter and granting our request. However, there is one little matter that remains to be dealt with yet. They sent the auditors to the various Canadian legions; I know they sent them to Calgary. They audited the accounts and said they were all right, took them back to Ottawa and we received word that they were confirmed. I should like to draw the attention of the government to the fact that they have failed as yet to send a cheque. It may be said it is only a little matter, but in my opinion it is rather important. I should appreciate it, very much, and I know that the Canadian legion would appreciate it, if the government would fulfil that promise and send a cheque to the various Canadian legions to pay the bills they have incurred for the burial of returned soldiers.
Last year the question of aviation occupied considerable time in this house. A promise was then made that civil aviation would be made entirely separate from military aviation. Some members to my right seemed to think that as the air force had done good work in the war, and so they did-they should necessarily continue in the force as regards civil aviation. I am glad that the government promised that civil aviation should be entirely separate from the Royal Air Force. There is, however, a feeling among the returned soldiers that the promise is not being carried out. It is true I received a letter from the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Ralston) intimating that as far as the private pilots were concerned they need not even be British subjects, that they might receive their certificates and be in no way obliged to be on the military reserve. Captain McColl, Canadian ace, who figured largely in the war, called me up and showed me his commercial certificate; and I may say that the returned [DOT]soldiers who are engaged in aviation at the present time are very anxious that a complete separation of the civil from the military force should take place. On Captain McColl's

certificate as a commercial pilot there is the statement that he is automatically on the Royal Air Force. I have a letter from the deputy minister stating that while that is in the regulation, it is a dead letter; it has not been carried out and probably will not be But in order to satisfy fully the returned soldiers I feel it is the duty of the government to say so; they should inform these men that, they are not in any way connected with the military force. The government will be well advised to take into consideration the suggestion of putting the civil aviation on a footing entirely separate from the national defence; it should be under either railways and canals or marine and fisheries.
I come no-w to the question of the returned soldiers. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that for various reasons I have a warm spot in my heart for returned soldiers. I may be wrong in my estimate, but I am certain of this: that there is a feeling among the returned soldiers, and there is a feeling in the Canadian legions at Calgary and Ottawa, that the returned men, when making application for reexamination,. or making appeals, do not meet with a sympathetic attitude on the part of those who are examining them. I am not positive that that is the case, but I know that the Canadian legions and many of the returned soldiers with whom I have conversed feel that way. Whether it is so or not I think the department and the hon. Minister of Health, (Mr. King, Kootenay) should give instructions that the medical men who examine our returned soldiers should at least be sympathetic and treat them as if they were equals, not as if the examiners were captains and the applicants privates in the department.
I cited last year for the benefit of the minister the case of a man who upon enlistment stated frankly-it was on his sheet-that he suffered from incipient Bright's disease, but he added: "I do not want to be a slacker;
I am here if you like to take me as I am." We took him. I say "we" because I was responsible along with other citizens of Canada. When he came back from the trenches his disease was aggravated-I mentioned that to my hon. friend the minister in the house last year. He applied for a pension. They brought down his files, told him it was a pre-war disability, and nothing was done about it. That case was fought from May, 1918, until 1927; for nine years it was considered, which shows how tardy and how unsympathetic, in some cases at any rate, the treatment of returned soldiers has been. And what is the result? Here is the result. I got word

The Address-Mr. Adshead
from the Canadian office, from the official adviser of the soldiers, who wrote me as follows:
No doubt you will remember this ease. The man was suffering from Bright's disease and was refused treatment or pension on the grounds that it was not aggravated on service. The man went to England and 1 was finally able to get the department to grant him pay and allowance. He received f50 this year.
After nine years' struggle they granted him pay and allowance; but when the postman took the letter down the street and knocked at the door the poor fellow lay in his coffin.
I could quote one or two other cases of that nature. I say there is either too much red tape or too much delay in these matters, and I submit, sir, that men who offered their lives for us on the fields of Flanders should receive far different consideration at our hands.
Now I come to immigration. Last session I had occasion to put some questions to the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) and he answered me along these lines:	I
can assure my hon. friend that there will be no flooding of labour in the towns and cities; all men who come here are going to farms either as farm help or as purchasers, and in six weeks from now there will be no unemployment. every man will be absorbed. I went home believing that, but as soon as I landed off the train in Calgary I saw three or four hundred Czechoslovakians walking the streets in search of jobs. They were willing to take anything they could get at from 25 to 30 cents an hour, to the detriment of Canadian workingmen. I wired to the Immigration department. We had been informed that an officer of the department, known as the superintendent of colonization, was supposed to look after immigrants on their arrival. I asked what his duties were. I was told he had to see that immigrants went to the places where they were supposed to go. But there was no superintendent of colonization accompanying these Czechoslovakians. They were brought in by the Canadian Pacific railway and landed at Calgary and other centres, where they were taking jobs at very low wages from Canadian workingmen anxious to secure work. Then I telegraphed the Prime Minister, and I wish to give him credit for his prompt attention, for he at once ordered an investigation. The investigator corroborated my statements in every respect. As soon as the investigator submitted his report the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart)-he was the Acting Minister of Immigration while the
minister of the department was away in England with Mr. Egan looking for more immigrants-I am informed cancelled the agreements with the railway companies, and thus put a stop to further immigration of this kind. I wish to give him and the Prime Minister every credit for their prompt action, but the point I want to bring out is this: We must have what I would term responsible immigration; and, further, the words of a minister given across the floor of the house that there is going to be no flooding of labour in our cities must be lived up to fully, to the very letter.
I think it was last session that I asked the Minister of Immigration:	Do you consult
at all with the provinces regarding their requirements for immigrants? And his reply was:	Well, not exactly. I hope that the
recent Dominion-provincial conference has changed that state of affairs. I think Mr. Brownlee's proposition is sound and would relieve the federal department entirely of responsibility if immigrants were brought in in excess of our requirements. He proposes: That it should be ascertained that immigrants coming in to buy farms have the necessary capital; that there should be a standard for the selection of immigrants; that in this selection the capacity of each province to absorb immigrants should be considered, and that the provincial authorities should advise the federal Department of Immigration in regard to their requirements. I think if the federal authorities would consult each provincial premier as to the class of men the province wanted, how many it wanted and when, the responsibility would be assumed by the provincial authorities, and the Department of Immigration would not be placed in the very unenviable position in which it found itself for a month or two last year. As I said before, I am very happy to give credit to the Prime Minister and the Acting Minister of Immigration for relieving the situation at that time as quickly as they could. At the last convention of the Alberta Federation of Labour it was stated that a large number of those Czechoslovakian immigrants were mechanics and knew nothing at all about farming, and that a number of them had secured work in the coal mines at Edmonton, thus depriving Canadians of work which they are rightfully entitled to. Before I came away the city of Calgary had incurred an expenditure of some five or six hundred dollars in looking after Czechoslovakians and Ukrainians who were sick and penniless and homeless in the city. I
The Address-Mr. Adshead

wrote to the Department of Immigration here asking if they would foot the bill, but they said there was no appropriation for the purpose. So the city of Calgary will have to pay for looking after people whom they had no voice in bringing to this country.
I entirely agree that the contented farmer is the best advertisement for immigration that Canada can have. [DOT] If you had farmers on the land who were prosperous and contented you could not keep immigrants out unless you put up a quota bar. To spend money and bring out men to settle on the land when those who are already here can barely make a living, is only going to increase the number of the discontented. We must make conditions on the land prosperous before we invite more settlers. I should like to see more immigrants from the British Isles, but as England is a highly industrialized country, and those in the rural centres do not seem very ready to leave the land, it follows that those who come here from the industrial centres are not exactly fitted to take up agriculture. A year ago a number of them came here from the mining districts, but they were entirely unsuited to our conditions, and for tin's reason some of them had to be deported.
As has been stated in this house before, what we require an immigration is quality rather *than quantity. I happened to meet Dr. Miller recently, at one time professor in the school of technology at Calgary. He went over to the United States and after three or four years returned to 'Calgary. He said, " Well, I have been three years in the United States, and they have almost made a pretty good Yankee of me." I replied, " That is too bad, Doctor. But will you tell me what are the qualifications to make a good Yankee that are not necessary to make a good Canadian?" In other words, the character of a man rather than his nationality is what counts. We have heard a good deal about foreign immigrants. I was present at a Canadian club meeting when a proposal was made to organize a Canadian club among the Ukrainians. A very laudable object, I suppose, but I think we are wrong if we suppose that because a man happens to have been bom m another country and speaks another tongue he does not appreciate and value Canadian institutions when he becomes a Canadian citizen. I hope none of us are labouring under such a great mistake, for the majority of our immigrants become good Canadians. I have in [DOT] mind a gentleman from Winnipeg whose father and mother, Icelanders, could not speak a word of English, yet he, their descendant, is a graduate of Manitoba

University, a Rhodes scholar, a member of this house, and a credit to Canada. I think my Canadian friends who were organizing the Canadian club were very much astonished when I told them of this fact. It is a very good thing to organize a Canadian club among the Ukrainians, but to assume an attitude of " I am holier than thou " or " I am better than thou " is rather beside the mark. I told them that in our house sitting quite near me was a gentleman, the hon. member. for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich), whose parents could not speak a word of English, who himself is a Ukrainian, who graduated with honours at Manitoba Law School and who is to-day a member of the House of Commons of Canada. Surely these things ought to show us that it is not necessarily nationality that tells as much as it is the character of the man whom we bring to this country. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) speak of the assimilation of different nationalities. I am strongly in favour of a mixture of those nationalities which, for certain physiological reasons, are capable of assimilating. I think Ruskin says something like this:
Every nation has within itself some peculiar characteristic which it alone has and which it alone can make as a contribution to building up civilization and each one of those characteristics should not be curbed but should be developed in order that in the building up of this human temple of civilization each one might produce its peculiar characteristics and give its contribution to the civilization of the day in which it lives.
I fear sometimes that when we meet with these people whom we call foreigners there is an attempt to submerge them, to tell them they must adopt our Canadian ideals. I value Canadian ideals; I value the Magna Charta;
I value the struggle for liberty; but I am sure my friends in Switzerland value William Tell just as much as I value corresponding heroes in Canadian history. When I went to the Ukrainian temple and saw the pictures on the wall I asked who they were, probably thinking they were some terrible bolshevists or communists. They pointed with pride to men who had straggled for liberty just as our nation had struggled for liberty. I did not attempt to disparage them. In valuing those ideals we must remember it is the ideal that counts, not so much the symbol that stands for it. That is my idea of the question, of immigration and assimilation. After all, what is it that makes the British nation strong? Were they all Anglo-Saxons to whom that strength is attributable? Not at all. It was the intermingling of those nations from

The Address-Mr. Adshead
northern Europe, Angles, Saxons, Normans, Jutes and Danes, that made the British a strong nation, and those countries which isolate themselves and keep themselves from everybody else are the ones that begin to decay.
I come now to the question of trade and commerce. I was very much interested [DOT] in reading the account of what the hon. member for West Calgary ,(Mr. Bennett) qaid in Vancouver. He is reported as having uttered these words:
We must decide within the next few years if we are to combine with other parts of the empire or combine with economic interests elsewhere. It is economic union within the British Empire or with our cousins to the south.
I notice tfhat he has advanced a stage in our relationship with the people to the south. They used to be " our neighbours " to the south; now they are "our cousins". He may get a closer relationship by and by. What I think my hon. friend ought to do is to state explicitly what he means by an economic union. If he means by an economic union; free trade within the empire, I will hold up both hands for it. I do not know whether he means that we are going to be forced into free trade with the United States or not.. I do not know that I would hold up both hands for that at the present time, but I would hold up both hands for a reduction in the tariff between this and other countries. But if by economic union within the empire he means freer trade and lower duties, he will have to settle with the manufacturers' association, because if there is anything that the manufacturers' association have fought before the tariff advisory board on occasions when I have heard them, it is the British preference. If we want economic union within the empire we must maintain the British preference to a greater strength than it is at the present time.
As regards the question of trade and commerce, I should like to know why we severed relations with Russia and why we destroyed trade which existed with Russia. I have never had an answer to that question. If the Russian people in Ottawa or in Canada generally have violated any confidence given to Canadians, if they have done wrong in Canada, I am quite willing to support the idea that for that reason we should sever diplomatic relations with those people. But if we severed relations with Russia simply because Mr. Baldwin did it or, as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) said last year, if we simply put up our umbrella because it is raining in London, then I say, as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St.' George (Mr. Cahan)
said this afternoon, that we are certainly exhibiting an inferiority complex. He was extremely desirous that Canada should settle Canadian affairs upon a purely Canadian basis or because purely Canadian interests were involved.
The1 hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) rather objected to the tariff advisory board. As both sides of the house agreed that the tariff advisory board was a very necessary institution in order, as they said, to take the tariff out of politics, I do not know what else we can do than seek to protect the ultimate consumers by presenting their case properly before that board. I am rather proud to say that I gave my little mite in order to keep Mr. Deaehman at the tariff advisory board as representing the consumers of this country. I am not at all ashamed of that fact. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) this afternoon brought out the fact that some of these people, made, during the year 1918, according to their own evidence, 291 per cent on the actual capital invested. The house will remember that the year 1918 was the time of greatest stress that Canada or Great Britain or the allies knew in fighting the Germans. That was the darkest year of the war. Extra duties were imposed upon cotton in order to raise revenue for war purposes, and at that particular time when we were in the greatest stress, when your boys and my boys were over yonder fighting for liberty, these gentlemen sitting in a directors' office in Montreal declared a profit of 291 per cent on the actual capital invested. It is no wonder that one gentleman who appeared before the cost of living committee said: "We are not running this business for the glory of God but for the profits of the shareholders ".
I may say in passing that I attended a banquet to the tenth battalion. Although I suppose I would be called a pacifist, I was proud to attend that banquet and to address the returned men. Sir Archibald Macdonell was there and confirmed my statement. When I spoke to those boys I made bold to make this statement, and I -make it now: If Canada is dragged into another war it will be against my strong personal opposition, and not simply because Mr. Baldwin or Mr. MacDonald says so. If that should occur, then so far as I am concerned we will strive for one thing more; no one in Canada will be allowed to stay at home and make huge profits while our boys are fighting in the trenches. We will all go to war, lawyers, doctors, and everyone else; we will all get $1.10 a day; no one will make these extor-
The Address-Mr. Adshead

tionate profits, and no one will get the richer the longer the war lasts. When I mentioned that fact at the banquet of the tenth battalion I was surprised at its reception. I said it rather hesitatingly, but every man jumped to his feet and cheered, and even Brigadier-General Macdonell said: " Put it there, old man; I agree with you ", I believe every returned soldier is against another war, but if it should come I know every man of them will insist on this condition and I will take the same stand.
I have one more word to say and then I am through. Last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) told us that no reductions were to be made in the tariff because no reports had been received from the tariff advisory board except on a few minor articles such as ep;om salts and so on, and he did not think it right or worth while to bring down any reductions in the tariff. I accepted that explanation at that time and voted for the budget precisely for that reason. Now the government can have no excuses of that sort; the .tariff advisory board has made fact finding reports in more cases than one. I see my friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) is not here. I am sorry, because when he was in Calgary he said that we in this corner attempted to foist our ideas upon the government and tried to bludgeon them. I do not want to use the bludgeon, but 'because I want to be true to my promises and true to the principles I enunciated in my nomination and my election. I said then that I was for low tariff and that I would support a low tariff; I must take a definite stand. I told the government last year that they could not run with the hare and hunt with the hounds. One of the members in that comer said last year that he believed in a high tariff, and I was very much astonished to hear that from the Liberal side. I wonder what Doctor Clark or Sir Wilfrid Laurier or Sir Richard Cartwright would have thought of that? If you believe in a high tariff, go to the side of the house where you belong, where there are other men who believe in it and where they advocate high protection. One vote either way does not mean very much, but I want to say that you must bring forth fruits meet for repentance. You now have reports from the tariff advisory board, and something concrete must be brought down; something must be put in the- budget to show that you meant what you said and that what was given given last year as a reason was not a mere excuse. Some reduction in the duties on the necessities of life must be made in the budget which is 
to come. If that is done according to your promise and according to the statements which you made last year, I shall be content to support your budget. But if there is nothing done by way of reducing the tariff; if there is nothing there to show that you have acted in good faith and in conformity with the facts found by the tariff advisory board, I am afraid I shall not be able to support your budget.
Mr. Speaker, I have finished my few remarks. I hope it will not be considered that I have been u ing the bludgeon, because in my criticisms I have not said anything in a vindictive way, and I hope my remarks will be taken in the spirit in which they are made.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I do so while suffering from a physical disability with which I have been slightly troubled of late, and. I may find it necessary to curtail my remarks. I shall confine myself, therefore, to one or two subjects in which I am vitally interested.
Much has been said during this debate with regard to the wonderful prosperity in Canada at present, and something has also been said as to the part played in that prosperity by the production last year of the second largest crop of wheat in our history. I believe this to be true, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to point out also that the farmers of Canada are not sharing in that prosperity in the proportion to which they are entitled. This, of course, is due to many reasons, one of the most important being the poor quality of the grain this year. As the hon. member who has just taken his seat mentioned, no matter what- the quality of the grain might be the handling charges remain the same; consequently the returns to the farmer this year are much less. In my opinion the main reason for this condition is the ravages of rust; this is true of the whole province of Manitoba, at any rate, and perhaps a large part of Saskatchewan as well. It is a condition which is not confined to rvheat alone; the oat crop over the area which I have mentioned was almost a complete failure last year, and that adds greatly to the difficulty of the farmer.
Just at this point I would like to give the government credit for the fact that they have established in Winnipeg a well-equipped and well-staffed laboratory for the purpose of studying and combating this rust menace. We have been alarmed, however, at statements, or rather rumors, issuing from an unknown source, to the effect that we are likely

The Address-Mr. Stexdsman
to lose the services of some of the most expert members of that staff because their salaries are not sufficiently large to induce them to stay. It would appear to me, Mr. Speaker, that a country holding the proud position of the greatest exporter of milling wheat in the world-for that is the position now held by Canada-can surely afford to engage and retain the services of the very best experts to be found anywhere in the world to combat 4 his menace. I have stated that the farmers are not reaping a sufficient reward for their labour, and I believe that if they are to continue in the production of such crops as have recently been harvested it is necessary they should be relieved from some of the burdens at least under which they are suffering at the present time.
It has been suggested during this debate that this session we may expect reductions in taxation. What form these reductions will take we have not been told, but I should like to point out that one of the greatest burdens from which the agriculturists of Canada are suffering is the protective duties. There was a discussion the other day as to whether or not the tariff is a tax. To my mind that is neither here nor there; if it is not a tax it is certainly a burden on the producers of this country. I do not wish at this time to discuss the tariff at length, but I must say that the agriculturists of Canada, particularly those in the west, are looking for reductions in the tariff on many of the articles that enter into the cost of living and the cost of production. And are they not justified in entertaining those expectations? My hon. friend the member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) pointed out this afternoon that last year the Finance minister made the boast that this government are a low tariff government and are proud of it. If that be so the people are justified in expecting reductions in the tariff this year.
Now I wish to discuss another point. A situation has arisen in my constituency which is perhaps common to other constituencies located, as it is, along the border line of the United States in the prairie country. Many of the residents of these constituencies immediately along the boundary line have had, for one reason or another, which is their own affair, occasion to cross over into the adjoining state of Dakota. In order to do so they secured a permit from the customs officials, and trouble has arisen because they have returned to their own homes, oftentimes late at night, instead of driving a further distance of twenty or twenty-five miles, as the case might be, in order to report to the officers 56103-10
and return their permits. That has resulted in heavy penalties and fines being inflicted upon men who were absolutely innocent of any desire to break the law, and a number of such cases have been brought to my attention.
I want it clearly understood that I am not seeking to defend smugglers or those engaged in smuggling. I am speaking to-night in the interest of innocent, honourable, law-abiding citizens who live on the Canadian side of the border. In the report of the royal commission on customs and excise various statements are made with which I agree. Among other things it 'is asserted that the customs offices in the west are not all located at the most- advantageous points from a strategical point of view, particularly in the province from which I come. The ports of entry are confined to the railway lines, which in many cases are a long way from the border, and this involves, of course, much extra travelling back and forth for the people who live between the custom houses and the border. Now I am quite sure that the minister (Mr. Euler) in framing the regulations responsible for these penalties, had no desire that innocent (people should suffer from them, and right here I want to do him the credit of saying 'that in every case in which I have appealed to him on behalf of innocent sufferers in my constituency he has Shown great .consideration and sympathy and has done hiis best to afford relief. But would it not be better in the interests of all concerned if such occurrences could be avoided? I think it is possible to prevent them from happening to a large extent.
Among other things the royal commission has suggested cutting out a number of the ports of entry, on the ground that there are too many of them in existence. That may be true; as to that I will not venture an opinion. I am convinced, however, that many of them are not located where they can best serve the objects for which they were called into existence. As I have already said, they are established along the railway lines, while the traffic between the. two countries in the particular locality to which I have reference is almost entirely by automobiles on the highway. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent, two provincial highways lead directly to the boundary line of the state of North Dakota, linking up there with highways on the other side and thus making it possible for international traffic to pass back and forth. I submit that is where the ports of entry should be located. Should the government see fit to consider this suggestion and put it into effect it will not only relieve

The. Address-Mr. Gershaw

the situation of which I have complained, but it will be of immense advantage to the travelling public who -pass backward and forward at the points in question, and will also provide a more efficient check on smuggling. It will make the smuggler's rvay harder and render it easier to -check him up and so stop this nefarious practice. The minister is not here tonight but I trust he will heed the suggestion I have made, because I am convinced that it would be of advantage, and I know positively that it would relieve the situation in regard to which I have had so many complaints from people living immediately along the boundary line.

I wish first of all to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address, who performed their task in an eloquent manner. It is no easy matter to begin a debate of this nature and they set a very high standard. As a member from Alberta I also wish to congratulate the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) on the high position which he now holds. The people of Alberta have a special pride in his success. When he returned from the Winnipeg convention the people in the different organizations in his home city of C-a-lgary gave him a welcome extending almost over a week. He was enthusiastically received in the capital city of Edmonton; in fact political and sectional differences were set aside and he was warmly applauded and honoured throughout the province.
The debate so far has been of a high order and free from unpleasant personal references. Many problems of national and international character have 'been discussed, and I hope to speak of some things of a more purely local nature. The leader of the opposition has presented the immigration problem as an issue. His words as reported at page 22 of Hansard, in reference to the getting in of new settlers read:
It cannot be done in any small way; it cannot be accomplished in any niggardly way, but is must be done in a large way. It involves the expenditures of vast sums of money and, more than that, it involves a large and comphensive policy of settlement.
Later on he pointed out that the province of Alberta had increased in -population from 1921 to 1926 to the extent of about 19,000; that is to say, it had increased from 588,000 to 607,000, or about three per cent. Who will say that we could properly assimilate a very much larger increase? At any rate, if that does seem small, I hardly think that the Liberal government here or the Progressive government in Edmonton should be blamed, because I believe the causes are

more economic than political. Let us see what some other agricultural districts have done during that same time. A census of some of the leading agricultural states in the American union shows an even smaller percentage of increase during the years from 1910 to 1920. Here are the actual figures: Kansas, an increase of five per cent in ten years; Iowa, five per cent; Kentucky, five per cent; Missouri, three per cent; North Dakota, ten per cent, and South Dakota, eight per cent. This is for a ten year period, and bear in mind that it covers the years from 1910 to 1920, during a considerable portion of which the war was in progress and prices were high, so that the drift was towards the farms. I cannot obtain the figures for the corresponding period from 1921 to 1926, but I think we may safely say that the rate of increase was *not very much greater, because those were the years.when there was a collapse in prices after the brief post-war boom; and they were the years of hard times in the farming districts both in the United States and in Canada.
As an illustration of the way in which prices have fallen, let us note that in February, 1920, the price of No. 1 Northern wheat was 82.15 whereas in 1921 it was $1.85; in 1922, $1.29, and in 1924, 99 cents. In other words, during that period the price of wheat had been more than cut in two. The price of coarse grains also followed the price of wheat. Now, the people had contracted certain obligations during these periods of high prices. Some men went on the land with the idea of producing food for the people of the world during the period of national crisis. When prices moved down these farmers found that they had to produce twice as much farm produce as they did before if they were to meet their obligations. Under such circumstances they were unable to carry on and many of them had to move out. Every one who has followed the trend of things in this country knows this to be true. Parliament itself officially recognized this state of affairs, for during the last session there rvas a revaluation of soldier lands. What was this but a recognition of the very fact which I have been stating?
Besides soldiers other settlers took up land during these times of peak prices and as their obligations were not reduced they encountered great difficulty in paying their way. During the past few years things have been a little better. The price of farm produce has increased, the prices of the things the farmers have to buy, machinery and Ford cars, have been reduced, and the price of

wheat has again advanced. But although there has been some measure of prosperity it is not as great as has been advertised. A good crop seemed to be almost within grasp of the people of southern Alberta but owing to unfavourable weather conditions only about fifty per cent of it could be threshed. Many people were unable to meet their obligations in respect of such relief as they had obtained during the long series of dry years and in respect also of commitments in connection with pre-emptions and interest on pre-emptions. If the people of the east knew how difficult it was for the people on the farms in the west to pay back the money advanced to them for fodder and relief they would agree with us that these old claims should be cancelled, as. should be also the interest on pre-emptions. The people of Canada as well as this government owe much to the men and women who now find themselves unable, through no fault of their own, to meet these obligations.
This year there has been widespread dissatisfaction over the grading of grain. The present arbitrary system depends to a great extent upon the judgment of the inspector; consequently it lacks scientific accuracy. There is on the order paper a resolution regarding this subject and I' assume that it will be fully debated later, but the producers would be glad if the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) would start an investigation with a view to working out some more satisfactory system of grading if this is at all possible.
Now, what policies should be adopted to modify or improve these conditions? I do not believe that bringing in a large number of immigrants at the present time would solve the problem unless living conditions are made happier for the people who are already here.
The cost of transportation must be as low as possible, and surely the Crowsnest pass agreement must be retained.
I do not think higher protection would help.

He says that the bureau of labour reports that employment is twenty per cent less than it was in 1920, and that there is a decrease of one-seventh in the payroll from 1920 to 1927. The index figure of employment in manufacture in 1920 was 118.8, and in 1926 it was 92.4. So we see that even in a country with a more highly protective tariff the condition has not been altogether good, and surely the condition would not be so good if the protection were increased in Canada, which is largely a producing country. We have a population of nine and a half millions and produce enough wheat to feed sixty millions. Many thousand cattle have been shipped to the United States this year in spite of the Fordney-McCumber tariff. I should say above all things that what we need as a primary requisite is a reduction in cost of living, and the one best means by which that can be secured is reduction of the tariff.
I recall with some interest the work of the tariff board. There have been a great many applications for tariff reductions. Many of the manufacturers have applied for tariff reductions because they are anxious to get their raw material at the lowest possible rate. Then there are a great many household articles of every day use on which reductions should be made. The average rate of duty upon enamel-ware and aluminum-ware is higher than upon silks and velvets, higher than upon jewellery, higher than upon fancy furs. The cotton schedule needs lowering in the worst possible way. It is so high now that it is stifling imports. Actual imports of cotton goods, measured in yards, on a per capita basis, are probably not more than one-half what they were in 1914. We cannot say that this is due to a change in the habits of dress of the people. There is a larger per unit consumption of cotton goods now than ever before. Merchants are appealing to the Minister of Finance to drop the sales tax. Millionaires are asking him to reduce the income tax, although few others favour its reduction. Revenues must be found, and I take the liberty of making this suggestion: a reduction in the rate of duty upon many items would be a considerable help in increasing the revenue. The rate is now so high that it constitutes an embargo upon imports, thus raising prices without making any material contribution to the revenue, with the result that the producers of this country are compelled to pay high prices and at the same time make contributions in other ways to the revenues, which under more reasonable conditions would come from customs taxes.

Raising tariff rates very frequently lowers actual revenue; reducing rates is apt to increase them.
In the milder climate of Alberta there are great numbers of horses, unused, running wild both winter and summer over the prairies. Since the war there has been little or no market for these horses, but the Department of Agriculture succeeded in selling about
3,000	of them to the Russian government during this year. The price is low, but otherwise no market could be found for the light horses. The horse owners appreciate the efforts of the Dominion and provincial departments of Agriculture and hope that these trade relations may be continued, as many more horses are available and every possible market for them should be developed.
Another problem much discussed in Alberta, and which means a great deal to returned men and others, is the getting of coal from the mines of that province to the markets of central Canada. This is such an important matter that boards of trade all over the country have passed many resolutions urging that something be done, and the government will make no mistake in taking the considered opinion and decisions of the men who make up these boards.
One other matter to which I wish to direct the attention of the government, and in which the west is tremendously interested, is that of branch line construction. There are many districts in western Canada in which rapid development is impossible because of the lack of railway facilities. In the constituency of Medicine Hat there are two branch lines required. One of them has been promised; very definite promises were made in regard to it several years ago. Many farmers have moved in and waited and waited, but as the line has not been completed they have had to move out. I realize the view held by some people in the east in regard to these matters. I have only this to say: in the older sections, where railway development has taken place, the resultant progress has certainly justified the act. I plead for generosity in the attitude of the house on this question. The history of Canada reveals a long record of struggle and doubt in regard to the wisdom of certain policies of railway construction. Sometimes we acted in haste; beyond question there were times when we built ahead of actual necessity, but taking into consideration the size of the country and the problems we had to face, we may pass lightly in judgment upon mistakes of the past. Railway building is not finished in Canada; it cannot be. If we are to make progress we must have a greater mileage than

we have at present, and if good judgment is exercised the construction of these branch lines will mean not greater burdens but the actual lifting of burdens now borne.
